steps.heading: Mixing Paint
steps.body:
Imagine you and a friend each pick a private color of paint. You want to agree on a shared secret color, but anyone watching the road between you sees every can you ship. The trick: you each mix your private color with a public color, swap the mixtures, then mix in your private color again on arrival. The eavesdropper watches mixtures go by but cannot un-mix paint.

Diffie-Hellman is that paint trick, except with numbers and a problem called the discrete logarithm. It is how two parties who have never spoken before agree on a shared encryption key over a hostile network. Every HTTPS handshake on Earth depends on some variant of this idea.

steps.heading: The Math
steps.body:
Both sides agree publicly on a large prime p and a generator g — these are not secret. Alice picks a private integer a, computes g^a mod p, and ships it. Bob picks a private integer b, computes g^b mod p, and ships it. Each side then raises the OTHER side's public value to their own private exponent.

Alice computes (g^b)^a mod p. Bob computes (g^a)^b mod p. Both land on g^(ab) mod p — the shared secret. To recover a or b from what crossed the wire, an attacker has to solve the discrete log problem in a 2048-bit prime field. That is not happening on any computer currently in existence.

Nothing called 'the secret' is ever transmitted. The secret is built in parallel on both ends from public material plus private knowledge.

steps.heading: Toy DH by hand
steps.body: Walk through the full exchange with numbers small enough to verify on paper. Same logic, same math, just smaller.
steps.code:
# Diffie-Hellman with toy numbers — small enough to follow by hand
p = 23                       # Public prime modulus (real ones are ~2048 bits)
g = 5                        # Public generator (a primitive root mod p)

# Alice picks her private key in secret and computes a public value
alice_private = 6
alice_public = pow(g, alice_private, p)   # g^a mod p

# Bob does the same on his end
bob_private = 15
bob_public = pow(g, bob_private, p)       # g^b mod p

# They swap publics over the wire. Eavesdroppers see these.
# Each side raises the OTHER side's public to their own private exponent.
alice_shared = pow(bob_public, alice_private, p)
bob_shared = pow(alice_public, bob_private, p)

print(alice_shared == bob_shared)         # True — same secret, never transmitted

steps.heading: Real-sized DH
steps.body: Toy numbers are for illustration. Production DH uses 2048-bit primes from RFC 3526 and a CSPRNG for the private exponent.
steps.code:
import secrets

# RFC 3526 group 14 — first 192 bits of a 2048-bit prime, abbreviated here
p = int("FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC90FDAA22168C234C4C6628B80DC1CD1", 16)
g = 2                                     # Standard generator for this group

# Cryptographically random private exponent in the range [1, p-2]
priv = secrets.randbelow(p - 2) + 1

# Compute the public value to send to the peer
pub = pow(g, priv, p)

# Suppose the peer's public arrived from the network
peer_pub = 0xDEADBEEFCAFE                 # Stand-in for the real value

# Derive the shared secret — never log this, never transmit this
shared = pow(peer_pub, priv, p)
print(f"shared secret bit-length: {shared.bit_length()}")

steps.heading: No Auth, No Trust
steps.body:
Diffie-Hellman gives you confidentiality from a passive eavesdropper. It gives you nothing against an active attacker sitting in the middle. Eve can intercept Alice's public, ship her own public to Bob, do the same in reverse, and end up with two shared secrets — one with each party. Both Alice and Bob think they have a secure channel. Eve decrypts and re-encrypts every message at her leisure.

This is why every real protocol bolts authentication onto DH. TLS signs the DH parameters with a certificate. SSH verifies the host key fingerprint. Signal uses long-term identity keys. Raw DH between strangers is a man-in-the-middle attack with extra steps.

Other traps: tiny private exponents (use a CSPRNG, not random.randint), non-prime moduli, small-subgroup attacks if you skip parameter validation, and recycling the same DH keypair across sessions. Use established libraries with vetted parameter sets unless you enjoy seeing CVE numbers next to your name.

steps.heading: Why Plain Hashes Lose
steps.body:
A breach hits the news every other week and the same line shows up: 'passwords were hashed.' Cool. Were they salted? Were they slow? Because if the answer is just 'SHA-256,' those passwords are already cracked.

A hash function is one-way: easy forward, hard backward. The trouble is, attackers do not need to reverse the function. They precompute the hashes of every common password, every dictionary word, every leaked password from prior breaches — millions of digests in a giant lookup table. Steal the hash database, run it against the table, score nine-tenths of the users in seconds. That table has a name: a rainbow table.

steps.heading: Salt and Cost
steps.body:
Two defenses turn this around. First, the salt — a random per-user value mixed into the hash. Now the same password yields a different digest for every user, and a precomputed table is useless because the attacker would have to rebuild it per salt. Salts do not need to be secret; they need to be unique.

Second, the cost — make each hash deliberately slow. Modern algorithms like bcrypt, scrypt, and Argon2 are tunable: bcrypt's cost factor doubles the work each step up; Argon2 lets you crank memory and parallelism. The legitimate server hashes once per login, no big deal. The attacker hashes a billion guesses, and now a billion times slow is the difference between cracking the database in an hour and cracking it in a century.

Use a password hash. Not SHA-256. Not MD5. Not your clever HMAC construction. A password hash.

steps.heading: How NOT to do it
steps.body: This is the bad pattern, documented so you can recognize it in a code review and replace it. SHA-256 is a beautiful hash function — for files, for blockchains, not for passwords.
steps.code:
import hashlib

# DANGER — this is the pattern that gets companies on the news
password = "hunter2"

# Encode to bytes because sha256 does not eat str directly
data = password.encode()

# Build the hash object and feed it the bytes
h = hashlib.sha256(data)

# Get the final digest as a hex string suitable for storage
digest = h.hexdigest()
print(digest)  # Same input always produces same output — rainbow table heaven

# A GPU rig will compute roughly 10 billion of these per second.
# A single $1500 box clears most password databases overnight.

steps.heading: Bcrypt the right way
steps.body: Bcrypt has been around since 1999 and it is still acceptable for new code. It bakes in the salt, includes a tunable cost factor, and refuses to be misused in obvious ways.
steps.code:
import bcrypt

# Bcrypt operates on bytes, not str
password = b"hunter2"

# Cost factor 12 = 2^12 rounds. Bump higher as hardware improves.
salt = bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=12)

# Hash — output bundles algorithm version, cost, salt, and digest in one string
hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(password, salt)
print(hashed)  # b'$2b$12$....'

# On login, verify with checkpw — constant-time comparison built in
guess = b"hunter2"
ok = bcrypt.checkpw(guess, hashed)
print(ok)      # True if the guess matches the stored hash

steps.heading: Traps and Variations
steps.body:
A few traps to file away. Bcrypt silently truncates inputs longer than 72 bytes — pre-hash with SHA-256 if you allow long passphrases, or pick Argon2id which has no such limit. Never compare hashes with `==` on your own; use the library's verify function so timing attacks do not leak which prefix matched.

A 'pepper' is a server-wide secret mixed in before hashing. It lives in your config or HSM, not the database, so a database-only breach does not expose hashes for offline cracking. Useful as defense-in-depth, never a replacement for a real password hash.

Work factors should migrate. The 2010 default is laughable in 2026. When a user logs in, check whether their stored hash uses your current cost; if not, re-hash with the new cost while you have the plaintext. And the eternal rule: do not invent your own scheme. The graveyard is full of 'I just SHA-256'd it twice with the username' designs.

steps.heading: Two Keys, One Trick
steps.body:
RSA is the asymmetric workhorse: one key encrypts, a different key decrypts. Hand the encryption key to the world, keep the decryption key locked up, and anyone can send you a message that only you can read. The same setup runs backwards for signatures — sign with your private key, anyone verifies with your public key.

The whole structure leans on a single hard problem: factoring large semiprimes. Multiplying two big primes is trivial. Recovering them from the product is the kind of hard that has resisted attack for half a century. Your private key is essentially 'I know the factors.' Your public key is essentially 'here is the product.'

steps.heading: The Key Schedule
steps.body:
You pick two large primes p and q. The modulus is n = p * q — that goes into the public key. Euler's totient phi = (p-1)(q-1) is needed for derivation but immediately discarded. The public exponent e is conventionally 65537, a small prime that makes encryption fast. The private exponent d is the modular inverse of e mod phi.

To encrypt m: ciphertext = m^e mod n. To decrypt c: plaintext = c^d mod n. The math collapses correctly because of Fermat's little theorem and the way d was chosen.

Key size matters. 1024-bit RSA is breakable by state actors. 2048-bit is the current floor. 3072-bit and up for anything that needs to stay confidential past 2030. And critically: textbook RSA — the raw formulas above — is broken in countless ways. You always wrap it in padding (OAEP for encryption, PSS for signatures) that adds randomness and structure.

steps.heading: Toy RSA by hand
steps.body: Walk the full key schedule with tiny primes so the arithmetic is checkable. Same math as the real thing, just within reach.
steps.code:
# Toy RSA — these primes are tiny enough to factor in milliseconds, never use IRL
p = 61
q = 53

# Public modulus — appears in every operation
n = p * q                    # 3233

# Euler's totient — used once, then immediately forgotten
phi = (p - 1) * (q - 1)      # 3120

# Public exponent — usually 65537, here 17 for legibility
e = 17

# Private exponent — modular inverse of e mod phi (Python 3.8+ native)
d = pow(e, -1, phi)

# Encrypt a message m where m < n
m = 123
ciphertext = pow(m, e, n)    # m^e mod n

# Decrypt with the private exponent
plaintext = pow(ciphertext, d, n)
print(plaintext)             # 123 — round trip succeeds

steps.heading: Production RSA
steps.body: Real code does not hand-roll the math. It uses a vetted library that picks safe primes, applies OAEP padding, and clears intermediate values. This is the shape of what production looks like.
steps.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa, padding
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes

# 2048-bit keypair — 3072+ for long-term confidentiality
priv_key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
pub_key = priv_key.public_key()

# Encrypt with OAEP — never use raw RSA or PKCS#1 v1.5 for new code
ciphertext = pub_key.encrypt(
    b"top secret payload",
    padding.OAEP(mgf=padding.MGF1(algorithm=hashes.SHA256()),
                 algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), label=None)
)

# Decrypt with matching padding parameters — mismatch raises an error
plaintext = priv_key.decrypt(ciphertext, padding.OAEP(
    mgf=padding.MGF1(algorithm=hashes.SHA256()),
    algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), label=None))
print(plaintext)

steps.heading: Where RSA Breaks
steps.body:
Textbook RSA — the raw `m^e mod n` from step 3 — is broken in production. With a small e and no padding, short messages can be recovered by taking the e-th root directly. Identical plaintexts produce identical ciphertexts, leaking information. Padding oracle attacks like Bleichenbacher's 1998 result against PKCS#1 v1.5 still take down servers that ignored 25 years of warnings. Always use OAEP for encryption and PSS for signatures.

Key generation has its own pitfalls. If two distinct RSA keys share a prime factor — which happens when entropy is weak at boot time — you can compute GCDs of public moduli and instantly factor both. This has been documented at scale across embedded device populations. Use a strong CSPRNG, and use the library's key generator.

RSA itself is slow on large payloads. The standard pattern is hybrid: generate a random symmetric key, encrypt the payload with AES-GCM, encrypt the symmetric key with RSA. RSA carries the key, AES carries the data.

steps.heading: Encrypt AND Authenticate
steps.body:
Encryption keeps data secret. Authentication proves data has not been tampered with. Run them separately and you eventually mess up the composition — one of the most common cryptographic foot-guns of the 2000s. AEAD ciphers solve this by doing both in one operation: Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data.

AES-GCM is the AEAD that runs the modern internet. Every TLS 1.3 connection, most VPN protocols, disk encryption on your phone — all GCM under the hood. It is fast, well-studied, and CPUs from the last decade have hardware instructions for it built right in.

steps.heading: Nonce, Tag, Galois
steps.body:
GCM combines AES in counter mode with a Galois-field authenticator. You provide three things: a key (typically 256 bits), a nonce (96 bits is the standard), and a plaintext. You optionally provide associated data — bytes that get authenticated but not encrypted, useful for headers, packet IDs, anything the receiver needs in cleartext but must verify.

The output is ciphertext plus a 128-bit authentication tag. The receiver, given the same key, nonce, and associated data, decrypts and verifies in one shot. If any byte is flipped — ciphertext, AAD, tag, anything — decryption fails loudly with an InvalidTag exception. No silent corruption.

The golden rule of GCM: a (key, nonce) pair must never repeat. Ever. Reuse a nonce under the same key twice and you have not only broken confidentiality of those two messages, you have leaked the authentication subkey and an attacker can forge arbitrary messages going forward. This is the single biggest mistake in real-world GCM deployments.

steps.heading: Encrypt and decrypt
steps.body: The minimum viable GCM round trip — generate a key, generate a nonce, encrypt, decrypt. The library handles the tag invisibly: appended to the ciphertext on encrypt, stripped on decrypt.
steps.code:
import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

# 256-bit key from a CSPRNG — AESGCM ships a helper for this
key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)
c = AESGCM(key)

# 96-bit nonce — GCM's recommended size. UNIQUE per (key, message).
nonce = os.urandom(12)

# Encrypt — output = ciphertext || 16-byte auth tag, concatenated
plaintext = b"the launch codes are 0000"
ct = c.encrypt(nonce, plaintext, None)

# Decrypt — raises cryptography.exceptions.InvalidTag on any tampering
recovered = c.decrypt(nonce, ct, None)
print(recovered)

# Receiver MUST pass the exact same AAD bytes or decrypt raises InvalidTag
pt = c.decrypt(nonce, ct, ad)
print(pt)

steps.heading: Nonce Reuse, the Career-Ender
steps.body:
There is exactly one rule you cannot break: never reuse a nonce with the same key. Two messages encrypted under the same (key, nonce) pair XOR to reveal the XOR of their plaintexts, which is often enough to recover both. Worse, in GCM specifically, nonce reuse leaks the authentication subkey H, after which an attacker can forge any message they like under that key.

Practical implications: do not generate nonces with a counter that resets after reboot. Do not derive nonces from message content. Do not let multiple threads share a counter without strict synchronization. Either use a 96-bit random nonce per message — collision probability is negligible at any sane volume — or use a deterministic counter that you are certain is monotonic across the entire lifetime of the key.

If you have any doubt about nonce uniqueness, look at AES-GCM-SIV or XChaCha20-Poly1305 — both tolerate nonce misuse better than vanilla GCM. And as always: rotate your keys. A single 256-bit AES key is good for about 2^32 messages before you should consider it tired.

steps.heading: The Tree
steps.body:
A Linux filesystem is a single tree starting at `/` — the root. Everything is somewhere under it. There is no C:\ or D:\; even external drives mount in as branches of the tree, usually under /mnt or /media. Your home directory hangs off /home, your user's stuff lives there, and configuration for the whole system sprawls across /etc, /usr, /var, /opt.

When you sit at a shell, the shell is always 'standing' in some directory — your present working directory. Every command you type runs relative to that location unless you say otherwise. Half of being effective on Linux is being aware of where you are standing and being precise about where you point.

steps.heading: Absolute vs Relative
steps.body:
A path that starts with `/` is absolute — it describes a route from the root of the tree, valid no matter where you currently stand. `/etc/passwd` always points to the same file. A path that does not start with `/` is relative — it is resolved from your current directory. `scripts/run.sh` means 'the scripts folder right next to me, then run.sh inside it.'

Two special names appear everywhere. A single dot `.` is the current directory. Two dots `..` is the parent. So `../logs` means 'one level up, then into logs.' And the tilde `~` expands to your home directory, no matter where you are. `~/.ssh/id_rsa` always points to the same file for a given user.

A few commands you will run thousands of times: `pwd` prints where you are. `ls` lists what is here. `cd` changes directory. Master those three and the filesystem opens up.

steps.heading: First steps
steps.body: The three commands you cannot do anything without. Run them in this order to get your bearings on any unfamiliar system.
steps.code:
# Print Working Directory — where am I standing right now?
pwd                          # /home/you

# List the contents of the current directory
ls                           # Names only, no fuss

# Long format: permissions, owner, size, modification time
ls -l                        # Now with detail

# Move into a subdirectory using a relative path
cd Documents                 # Working directory is now ./Documents

# Move up one level with the parent-directory shortcut
cd ..                        # Back to the previous spot

# Jump straight to your home directory from anywhere on the system
cd ~                         # ~ expands to /home/you

# cd with no argument is identical — same effect, jumps home
cd                           # Identical to 'cd ~'

steps.heading: Hidden files, absolute paths
steps.body: Once you can move around, you need to see the things ls hides by default and reach places that are not nearby. This is the next layer.
steps.code:
# Hidden files begin with '.' — ls skips them unless told
ls -a                        # -a includes .bashrc, .ssh, .config, ...

# Combine flags: long format AND hidden files. Classic recon listing.
ls -la                       # The two-second 'what is going on here'

# Absolute paths start with / and ignore your current location
cd /etc                      # Drops you in /etc regardless of starting point

# Inspect a directory without moving into it
ls /var/log                  # Useful when you just want a peek

# Tilde works inside any path, not just on its own
ls ~/.ssh                    # Look at your SSH config if it exists

# Combine relative pieces with .. for sibling directories
ls ../scripts                # The 'scripts' folder one level up

# cd - jumps back to your previous directory (handy flag)
cd -                         # Toggle between two recent locations

steps.heading: Sharp Edges
steps.body:
Filenames with spaces will betray you. `cd My Documents` tries to cd into two arguments — `My` and `Documents` — and fails on both. Quote them: `cd "My Documents"` or escape the space: `cd My\ Documents`. Same goes for filenames with parentheses, ampersands, or any shell metacharacter.

The parent shortcut `..` at the root level is still `/` — you cannot escape upward past root. Symbolic links can lie about the tree's shape: `cd` follows symlinks by default and `pwd` reports the symlink path, while `pwd -P` reports the real one. On a tangled filesystem the difference matters.

Finally, two ergonomic habits. Tab completion is your reflex — half-type a name, hit Tab, let the shell finish it. You will type fewer wrong paths and discover filenames you forgot existed. And `cd` with no arguments goes home, every shell, every distro. Memorize the muscle: `cd <Enter>` is a panic button.

steps.heading: Knowledge Check
steps.question: You SSH into a server, run `pwd`, and see `/var/www/sites/blog`. You want to inspect the SSH authorized_keys file for the current user. Which command gets you there most reliably regardless of where you happen to be standing?
options: cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
cat ./.ssh/authorized_keys
cat ../.ssh/authorized_keys
cat .ssh/authorized_keys
steps.hint: Your current directory could be anywhere on the system. Which path notation does not care where you are standing?
